docs.title: HIVE
docs.text:
Hydrodynamic Identification and Validation Environment

HIVE is a Python framework for wave energy converter (WEC) hydrodynamic modelling, identification, and model benchmarking.

docs.title: What HIVE does
docs.text:
HIVE provides structured pipelines to:

  • Process CFD simulation data
  • Validate existing physics and data-based models against CFD reference data
  • Identify model parameters and data-driven surrogates from CFD reference data

docs.title: Key features
docs.text:
• BEM-based linear and weakly-nonlinear hydrodynamic model
  • Viscous drag identification
  • PI gain identification for PTO control
  • Multiple and various data-based model (wave-to-force-to-velocity state-space, system identification for nonlinear dynamic (SINDY), neural network)
  • model benchmarking through large metric bank

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• environment surrogate
  • A HydroSphere BEM pickle file (r5.pkl is the project default) placed under source/models/bem/ for validation and/or identification pipeline
  • A reference raw dataset folder for placed under 'data/cfd/' for handle pipeline
  • A reference handled dataset (.csv) for validation and identification pipeline placed under data/handled/
  • A model (.json) for validation and/or identification pipeline placed under source/models/

docs.title: Quick test run
docs.text:
All scripts are run as modules from inside the code/ folder. A minimal test case is provided using r5.pkl as BEM model and out_Case_65_20_120000_-430000_example as raw reference dataset. Run it with: 

# 1 — process CFD data
python -m script.run_handle_data --case example_cases.json

# 2 — validate models
python -m script.run_validate --case example_validate.json

# 3 — identify parameters
python -m script.run_identify --case example_identify.json

Outputs land in data/handled/example_cases/ (handle data), out/validated_case/example_validate/ (validate), or models/example_identify/identification/ for identification results (identify). When repeating the test run again, a user command is required, choose [1] erase and redo all. More information is available in the user manual.

docs.text:
This documentation is based on mkdocs and is mostly a log for the code author rather than a package documentation for external users.

To update the documentation, mkdocs gh-deploy should be ran in code/doc/

docs.title: Pipeline Overview
docs.text: HIVE is built around three pipelines ran via scripts, run_handle_data, run_validate and run_identify, each driven by a JSON input file and writing outputs to a structured folder.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
Script What it does Config location Output location run_handle_data Reads raw CFD time series, applies cut times and optional resampling, computes wave parameters and hydrodynamic quantities, saves one processed dataset per case inputs/handle_case/<name>.json data/handled/<name>/ run_validate Loads processed datasets and a model.json, runs forward simulations via SimRun, computes metrics against the CFD reference, produces scatter plots over the \((H_s, T_e)\) parameter space inputs/validate_case/<name>.json out/validated_case/<name>/ run_identify Uses a scheme module (viscous_drag, pi_gain, or linear_si) to identify model parameters from CFD data, updates model.json with the result inputs/identify_case/<name>.json models/<name>/ + models/<name>/identification/

Each script read the input .json file --case <name>.json argument. The stem of that filename becomes the output folder name — choose stems that are short, lowercase, and use underscores (e.g. r5_reg).

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Every plot is saved as both .png (for quick viewing) and .pkl (interactive Matplotlib figure). Reload a .pkl interactively with option [3] at the rerun prompt, or directly:

import pickle, matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig = pickle.load(open("plots/sea_state.pkl", "rb"))
plt.show()

docs.title: run_handle_data
docs.text: Processes raw CFD time series into a standardised format ready for validation and identification.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
python -m script.run_handle_data --case <name>.json

Config files ´.json´ live in inputs/handle_case/. The filename stem becomes the output folder name under data/handled/.

docs.title: Rerun options
docs.text:
When the output folder already exists, the script prompts:

[1] erase and redo all     — reprocess + replot from scratch
[2] stop, do nothing
[3] load saved figures     — reopen existing .pkl plots interactively
[4] remake figures only    — reuse processed CSVs, regenerate plots

Option [4] is useful when tuning plot parameters without reprocessing data.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
1. Reads each CFD case folder from data/cfd/
  2. Instantiates a DataHandle object per case
  3. Calls processData() — computes radiation force, hydrostatic force, linear excitation force (fe_lin), and absorbed power
  4. Optionally resamples to a target dt
  5. Saves processed data and wave parameters to data/handled/<name>/data/
  6. Generates and saves plots to data/handled/<name>/plots/

docs.text:
{
  "wave_type": "regular",
  "cut_time": [50, 0],
  "duration": null,
  "hydro_sphere_pkl": "r5",
  "dt": 0.05,

    {
      "T": 8.0,

    "sea_state": true,
    "power": true,
    "dynamics": true,
    "hydro": false,
    "3d": false,
    "variable": ["fe_lin", "x"]

}

docs.title: Case labels
docs.text:
Each CFD case is assigned a label derived from its parameters. The label is used as the CSV filename stem and as the series label in plots:

Hs{H}p{dec}_Te{T}p{dec}_d{damping}_k{stiffness}

Example: Hs2p0_Te8p0_d120000_k-280000

An optional "tag" field in the case config appends a suffix: Hs2p0_Te8p0_d120000_k-280000_example.

docs.text: Key Description sea_state Wave spectrum and elevation time series power Absorbed power time series and grid dynamics Displacement, velocity, and phase plot hydro Hydrodynamic force breakdown 3d 3D scatter over sea state space variable Any named column — list of column names, one plot each

docs.title: run_identify
docs.text: Identifies model parameters or data-driven surrogates from CFD reference data using a pluggable scheme system.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
python -m script.run_identify --case <filename>.json

Config files live in inputs/identify_case/. The filename stem becomes the output folder name under models/.

docs.title: Available schemes
docs.text: Scheme key Module What it identifies viscous_drag Viscous_drag.py Quadratic drag coefficient \(c_v\) via least-squares pi_gain Pi_gain.py PI controller gains \(K_p\), \(K_i\) linear_si Linear_si.py \(\eta \to f_e\) and \(f_e \to \dot{x}\) state-space models via VF or N4SID

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
1. Loads the base model definition from models/<base_model>/model.json
  2. Creates a DDFeed — loads training DataHandle objects and runs scheme.prep()
  3. Creates an Optimizer — owns simulation helpers and delegates to scheme.run()
  4. Saves identified parameters, result JSON, simulation CSVs and plots

docs.title: Config fields
docs.text: See Input Config Reference — identify.

docs.title: Rerun options
docs.text: Option Action [1] Erase and redo [2] Stop [3] Reload saved figures [4] Save results with today's date suffix (keeps existing folder)

docs.text:
models/<name>/
├── model.json          ← updated with identified parameters
├── run.log
└── identification/
    ├── result.json
    ├── data/
    │   └── *.csv
    └── plots/
        └── *.png / *.pkl

def prep(feed: DDFeed): ...
def run(opt: Optimizer, feed: DDFeed, config) -> tuple: ...
def save(opt: Optimizer, result: dict, output_name: str): ...
def log_result(result: dict): ...
def save_data(result, simruns, grids, feed, data_dir): ...

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The base model must exist at models/<base_model>/model.json before running.
  • t_warmup and t_causal are computed from the base model and applied to all simulation clips automatically.
  • For linear_si, the scheme loads its own signal data (SELF_LOADING = True) and does not use CFD DataHandle objects.

docs.title: Solver config
docs.text:
Each entry in solvers has the following fields:

Field Type Description method string "RK4", "RK2", or "euler" dt float Integration timestep [s] interpolation dict Per-force-term interpolation flags (see below)

docs.title: interpolation
docs.text:
The precomputed force signals (\(f_e^{lin}\), nonlinear FK force, wave elevation) are evaluated on the handled data grid. During ODE integration, sub-stage evaluations may fall between grid points. The interpolation dict controls, for each force term, whether it is re-evaluated at every RK sub-stage or frozen to the value at the start of the step (zero-order hold).

The underlying grid interpolation is always piecewise linear.

Key Force term Effect when true "fe" Linear excitation force \(f_e^{lin}\) Evaluated at each RK sub-stage "fk" Nonlinear Froude–Krylov force Evaluated at each RK sub-stage "eta_hs" Wave elevation for nonlinear hydrostatic Evaluated at each RK sub-stage

Setting a key to false freezes that term within each timestep (ZOH), which is cheaper but reduces effective accuracy for that term. An empty dict {} enables interpolation for all terms and is recommended for RK4 and RK2.

"interpolation": {}                        // all terms interpolated (default)
"interpolation": {"fe": false}             // freeze excitation force, interpolate rest
"interpolation": {"fe": false, "fk": false} // freeze both, interpolate eta_hs only

docs.title: solver.interpolation
docs.text:
The excitation force \(f_e^{lin}\) and wave elevation are precomputed on the handled data grid. At each ODE stage the solver evaluates them at intermediate time points via interpolation. The interpolation dict is passed to scipy.interpolate.interp1d:

"interpolation": {}               // default — linear interpolation
"interpolation": {"kind": "linear"}   // same as above, explicit
"interpolation": {"kind": "nearest"}  // zero-order hold (step function)
"interpolation": {"kind": "cubic"}    // cubic spline, smoothest
kind value Behaviour "linear" Piecewise linear (default, recommended) "nearest" Zero-order hold — holds value at nearest grid point "quadratic" Quadratic spline "cubic" Cubic spline — smoothest, highest cost

Using "nearest" with RK4 reduces the effective accuracy of the forcing term to first order. "linear" is a good default for all solver methods. See Models & Solvers — Forcing signal interpolation for a full discussion.

docs.title: Metric names
docs.text:
Metrics passed in the metrics list of validate and identify configs follow this pattern:

Name Description nrmse_x NRMSE on displacement nrmse_xdot NRMSE on velocity rmse_x RMSE on displacement [m] rmse_xdot RMSE on velocity [m/s] mean_P_abs Mean absorbed power [W]

See Metrics for definitions.

docs.title: Model types
docs.text:
A model in HIVE is a folder under models/ containing a model.json file. The JSON records the model's physics components, identified parameters, and metadata. Currently supported model types:

Model key Description linear Cummins equation with radiation state-space, linear PTO linear_viscous As linear, plus quadratic drag $c_v

Models identified by run_identify inherit a base model's model.json and add or update the identified parameters.

docs.title: model.json structure
docs.text:
{
  "type": "linear_viscous",
  "hydro_sphere_pkl": "r5",
  "radiation": {
    "A": [[...], ...],
    "B": [[...]],
    "C": [[...]],
    "D": [[...]]
  },
  "hydrostatic": {
    "K_hs": 142000.0
  },
  "added_mass_inf": 450.0,
  "mass": 1200.0,
  "c_v": 1850.0,
  "t_warmup": 15.0,
  "t_causal": 3.2
}

The radiation block holds the state-space matrices \((A_{rad}, B_{rad}, C_{rad}, D_{rad})\) fitted from the BEM IRF. These are written by run_handle_data during the first call that initialises the BEM data.

docs.title: SimRun
docs.text:
SimRun is the class responsible for running a single forward simulation. It:

  1. Loads the model definition from model.json
  2. Instantiates the radiation state integrator
  3. Steps the ODE forward using the chosen solver
  4. Returns a dataset attribute (a pandas.DataFrame) with the same column schema as DataHandle

Because SimRun and DataHandle expose the same .dataset and .label interface, they can be mixed in plotter calls.

docs.title: ODE solvers
docs.text:
The solver block in validate and identify configs selects the numerical integrator:

"solver": {
  "method": "RK4",
  "dt": 0.05,
  "interpolation": {}
}
Method Description RK4 4th-order Runge–Kutta (recommended) RK2 2nd-order Runge–Kutta (Heun's method) euler Forward Euler (1st order, fast but inaccurate)

The integration timestep dt is independent of the CFD data's native timestep. HIVE interpolates the forcing signals (wave elevation, excitation force) onto the solver grid using the scheme specified in interpolation.

docs.title: Warmup period
docs.text:
The radiation state-space system starts at rest (\(\mathbf{z}_{rad} = 0\)). It takes several wave periods for the radiation states to converge to their quasi-steady values. HIVE computes t_warmup automatically from the pole magnitudes of \(A_{rad}\):

\[ t_{warmup} = \frac{-\log(\epsilon)}{\min_k |\text{Re}(p_k)|} \]

where \(\epsilon\) is a small tolerance (default \(10^{-3}\)) and \(p_k\) are the eigenvalues of \(A_{rad}\). The value is logged in run.log and saved in result.json.

Metrics are computed only over \([t_{warmup},\; T_{end} - t_{causal}]\).

docs.title: Why interpolation is needed
docs.text:
The excitation force \(f_e^{lin}\) and wave elevation \(\eta\) are precomputed on a fixed grid — the timestep of the handled CFD data (set by dt in the handle config). The ODE solver may use a different timestep. At each stage of the integrator (e.g. the four stages of RK4), the forcing signals must be evaluated at intermediate time points that generally do not fall on the original grid, requiring interpolation.

Note that \(f_e^{lin}\) is state-independent — it does not depend on \(x\) or \(\dot{x}\) — so it is fully precomputed before integration begins. This is unlike the radiation force \(f_{rad}\), which is stepped forward as a state-space system at each stage, or \(f_{hs}\) and \(f_{pto}\), which are evaluated from the current state.

docs.title: Interpolation schemes
docs.text:
The interpolation dict in the solver config is passed directly to scipy.interpolate.interp1d via the kind keyword:

kind Description Accuracy "linear" (default) Piecewise linear between grid points 2nd order in grid spacing "nearest" Zero-order hold — value at nearest grid point 1st order (step function) "quadratic" Piecewise quadratic spline 3rd order "cubic" Piecewise cubic spline 4th order

docs.title: Consistency with the ODE solver
docs.text:
A subtle point: if you use RK4 ("method": "RK4") but hold the forcing constant within a step ("kind": "nearest"), the integration is effectively first-order in the forcing term. The radiation and restoring forces benefit from the full RK4 accuracy, but the excitation forcing does not. For best results, match the interpolation order to the solver:

  • RK4 / RK2: use "linear" or "cubic"
  • Euler: "nearest" (ZOH) is sufficient and cheapest

In practice, "linear" is a good default — it is cheap and ensures that \(f_e^{lin}\) varies smoothly across RK stages.

docs.title: Practical note on grid resolution
docs.text: The interpolation error decreases as the handled data timestep decreases. If you notice artefacts in simulated time series (especially at high frequencies), try reducing dt in the handle config to produce a finer forcing grid, rather than switching to a higher-order interpolation scheme.
